theme_scores.theme: Shifting costs to the landlord market
theme_scores.justification: The core claim is supported by the Scottish evidence (Ref 16) showing agencies raising landlord fees (17%) and letting agent numbers rising (more competition), with the document explicitly assessing that 'agents, in order to remain competitive, are unlikely to pass the full costs of the fees onto landlords' and noting the comparison is imperfect ('it is difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets').

theme_scores.theme: Benefits to tenants from a clear ban
theme_scores.justification: The specific tenant benefits (comparing properties, saving for a deposit) are asserted without evidence; the only loosely related evidence, that '56% of private tenants agreed... not being able to charge fees... improves the rental sector' (Ref 16), is not explicitly tied to these specific benefits.

The claim that scope must cover agents, landlords and third parties is backed only by the vague, uncited line 'there is evidence that... some agents are double charging landlords and tenants', which is mentioned but not sourced or elaborated.

This theme cites a named report (Ref 16, Shelter/Rettie/BDRC) with specific findings (e.g. 'between 1% and 2% of the rent rises... could, in part, be caused by the law on fees, this is inconclusive') and explicitly acknowledges limitations ('it is difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets').
States the policy's aims (Ref 2, Autumn Statement) and government preferences with no evidence of why a ban was chosen to meet them.

Describes the Scottish 2014 Act's features as a model but only as description of current rules, not as evidence of effectiveness, aside from a general claim that it will 'help strengthen the letting agent industry' without data.
Purely descriptive of the 1984 and 2011 Acts' legal provisions, with no assessment of their effects or link to choices made for the English ban.
Purely descriptive summary sentences with no evidence offered.

reasoning: The four core themes vary sharply in evidential grounding. 'Scottish precedent' (level 3) is the strongest: it names a specific report (Ref 16, Shelter/Rettie/BDRC), gives figures (e.g. '1% and 2% of the rent rises... inconclusive', '17% of agencies claim to have increased fees to landlords'), and explicitly flags uncertainty and limits to comparability ('it is difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets'). 'Shifting costs to the landlord market' also reaches level 3, since this same Scottish evidence directly supports its claim that landlords will absorb costs while agents compete harder, and the document assesses this with nuance ('agents... are unlikely to pass the full costs of the fees onto landlords'). 'Benefits to tenants' (level 1) and 'Comprehensive scope' (level 1) rest mostly on unevidenced assertion or vague unnamed claims ('there is evidence that... some agents are double charging'), with no citation or clear link to the specific claims made. The mean of the four core levels (3, 1, 1, 3) is 2.0, giving a section score of 2. The strongest counter-example is that the apparently richest evidence (the Scottish report) is borrowed from a different theme, and its link to 'comprehensive scope' and 'tenant benefits' is weak or absent. To reach level 3 overall, the document would need to cite evidence directly supporting tenant-side benefits and the necessity of comprehensive scope, with the same kind of sourced, assessed detail given to the Scottish rent evidence.
